title: Option B Diverse Voices Audition — 6 Real-Actor Podcaster Voices Across 3 Duos

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: Meet 6 studio-recorded human podcast hosts (Dublin, West Coast, Northwest, Vancouver, Glasgow & Sydney) riffing on sodium-channel sparks, the 20-watt brain, and ancient medical detectives.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Long deep dives stay way more engaging when each series has its own distinct, genuinely human co-host chemistry instead of the same two voices every time.
keyTakeaways: Duo 1 (Liam · Dublin & Claire · West Coast): How a single SCN8A amino acid swap leaves a 1% persistent sodium trickle in NaV1.6.
Duo 2 (Marcus · Northwest & Nora · Vancouver NPR): How 3 pounds of brain switch rules on 20 watts—less than a fridge bulb.
Duo 3 (Callum · Glasgow & Tessa · Sydney): How Sushruta's ancient 'honey urine' observation connects straight to modern SGLT2 cryo-EM.

vocab.meaning: The main voltage-gated sodium channel at a neuron's starting line that fires electrical action potentials.
A tiny ~1% sodium leak when a channel gate doesn't fully latch shut, making neurons re-fire.
The kidney's molecular pump that normally pulls glucose back into blood before it spills into urine.

quiz.question: In Duo 1, what happens when the N1768D mutation hits the NaV1.6 sodium channel?
options: The channel completely disappears from the neuron
About 1% of the sodium current fails to shut off, pushing the neuron back toward firing
The neuron freezes and stops using ATP
quiz.explanation: Even a 1% persistent sodium trickle acts like a leaky faucet that keeps depolarizing the axon initial segment.

quiz.question: Roughly how much electrical power does the human brain use according to Duo 2?
options: About 20 watts (like a dim refrigerator bulb)
quiz.explanation: Despite running complex rule-switching and consciousness, the human brain runs on roughly 20 watts of metabolic power.

transcript.speaker: Liam (en-ie-podcaster-2)
transcript.text: Okay, Claire, wait—stop me if I have the scale wrong here. We're talking about NaV1.6, this tiny voltage-gated sodium channel sitting right at the axon initial segment, yeah?

transcript.speaker: Claire (en-us-podcaster-11)
transcript.text: Right at the ignition switch of the neuron. Yeah. And the wild thing is, normally that gate snaps open for—what, less than a millisecond?—and then boom, the hinged lid slams shut.

transcript.speaker: Liam (en-ie-podcaster-2)
transcript.text: <laugh> Less than a millisecond! And in this SCN8A mutation, N-seventeen-sixty-eight-D, you swap literally one amino acid—one!—and the latch just... doesn't quite catch?

transcript.speaker: Claire (en-us-podcaster-11)
transcript.text: That's it! <short pause> Just a tiny trickle—like one percent of the sodium current refuses to turn off. It's like a kitchen faucet that won't quite seat on the washer, except inside a brain cell, that tiny drip keeps pushing the membrane right back to threshold, firing again and again.
transcript.highlightSummary: 1% persistent Na+ leak drives repetitive firing

transcript.speaker: Marcus (en-us-podcaster-1)
transcript.text: Here's the number that always breaks my brain, Nora. A frontier data center pulls megawatts—enough electricity to light up a small town—just to predict the next word.

transcript.speaker: Nora (en-ca-podcaster-2)
transcript.text: Mm-hmm. And meanwhile, you're sitting there with three pounds of warm, salty tissue inside your skull, running on twenty watts. Like... a dim refrigerator bulb.

transcript.speaker: Marcus (en-us-podcaster-1)
transcript.text: <sigh> A dim fridge bulb! And yet, when someone changes the rules of the game mid-sentence—like in Berg and Grant's Wisconsin Card Sorting Test—your prefrontal cortex flips the entire rule set in half a second.
transcript.highlightSummary: Human dlPFC switches rules on 20 watts vs megawatt AI

transcript.speaker: Nora (en-ca-podcaster-2)
transcript.text: <laugh> Well, provided your dopamine D1 receptors are in that Goldilocks zone, right? Too little signal and the circuit drifts; too much stress and the whole network locks onto the old rule and won't let go.

transcript.speaker: Callum (en-gb-podcaster-8)
transcript.text: People love to laugh at ancient doctors, Tessa, like they were all just guessing in the dark with leeches and star charts.

transcript.speaker: Tessa (en-au-podcaster-1)
transcript.text: Oh, totally unfair! Take Sushruta in ancient India describing 'honey urine'—madhumeha—watching ants march straight toward a patient's sample. That's literally a bedside glucose assay three thousand years before lab strips!

transcript.speaker: Callum (en-gb-podcaster-8)
transcript.text: <laugh> Aye, and fast-forward to modern cryo-EM—now we can actually zoom in to three ångströms and watch the exact transporter in the kidney, SGLT2, getting overwhelmed when blood sugar spikes.

transcript.speaker: Tessa (en-au-podcaster-1)
transcript.text: Exactly. Same human physiology, same overflow valve—just three millennia between noticing the ants on the clinic floor and photographing the molecular lock that lets the sugar spill.
transcript.highlightSummary: Ancient bedside signs map directly onto modern cryo-EM transporters
